This vignette demonstrates the basic usage of the statomatic package to analyze data from an experiment.

It includes three analyses, showing how statomatic handles different experimental designs: a multi-group (> 2) two-factor design, a two-group one-factor design, and a multi-group one-factor design.

First, load the statomatic package.

```{r setup}
library(statomatic)
```

## How statomatic chooses a test

Statomatic tests each row of the data (each gene, taxon, metabolite, ...) separately. For every row it first checks whether the residuals of a linear model are normally distributed (Shapiro-Wilk test) and whether the groups have equal variances (Levene test). This sorts the rows into three sets:

| Set | Meaning | 2 groups | > 2 groups | > 2 groups: pairwise comparisons |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ne | normal, equal variance | t-test | ANOVA | Tukey HSD |
| nu | normal, unequal variance | Welch test | Welch test | Dunnett T3 |
| nn | not normal | Wilcoxon test | Kruskal-Wallis test | Dunn test |

Each set is then analyzed with the tests suited to it, and fold changes are calculated between every pair of groups.

## Part 1: Multi-group, two-factor design

The data analyzed here is from an RNA sequencing experiment which aimed to identify differentially expressed genes across several experimental conditions. The details of this experiment won't be discussed here.

Load the data to be analyzed. Here we analyze the normalized counts, as created by DESeq2.

```{r data_read-in}
norm_counts <- read.csv("normalized_counts.csv")
head(norm_counts)
```

Notice that the row names of norm_counts are numbers, and that the gene ids are actually inside the data.frame. Statomatic can only analyze numbers, so the gene ids need to be the row names, and the gene id column needs to be removed.

Statomatic has a built-in function for this, `cf()`. It sets a specified column of a data.frame as the new row names, and then removes that column from the data.frame. The column can be chosen with `column_index`, which defaults to 1 (the first column).

Using `cf()` with the default `column_index = 1` is the same as reading the file with `read.csv("normalized_counts.csv", row.names = 1)`. Either way works; `cf()` is handy when the data is already loaded.

```{r column_fix}
norm_counts <- cf(norm_counts)
head(norm_counts)
```

Now the data is ready to be analyzed.

We also need to tell statomatic which experimental conditions each sample belongs to. We do this with a data.frame, `sample_info`, with one row per sample: a column with the sample names (the column names of norm_counts), and one column per experimental condition. The experimental conditions here are sex and genotype.

```{r make sample info}
sample_info <- data.frame(sample = colnames(norm_counts),
                          sex = c(rep("Male", 10), rep("Female", 10)),
                          genotype = c(rep("WT", 5), rep("KO", 5), rep("WT", 5), rep("KO", 5)))
sample_info
```

Statomatic matches the rows of `sample_info` to the columns of the data by sample name, so the order of the rows doesn't matter. It finds the column with the sample names automatically (here, `sample`). If your sample names are the row names of `sample_info` instead, that works too.

Now we run the analysis with `multigroup_main()`. We give it the data, `sample_info`, and the names of the columns of `sample_info` to use as the experimental factors.

```{r run multigroup_main}
set.seed(1)
res <- multigroup_main(norm_counts, sample_info, factors = c("sex", "genotype"))
```

With two factors, statomatic uses a two-way ANOVA for the normal, equal-variance (ne) rows. The pairwise comparisons and fold changes compare every combination of the factors: statomatic combines sex and genotype into four groups (Female_KO, Female_WT, Male_KO and Male_WT).

The Dunnett T3 test calculates its p-values with a random (Monte Carlo) method, so its p-values can change very slightly from one run to the next. Setting a seed with `set.seed()` before the analysis makes the results reproducible.

The result is a list:

```{r names}
names(res)
```

- `anova_results`, `welch_results` and `kw_results` hold the results for the ne, nu and nn rows.
- `foldchanges` holds the fold changes and group means of every row.
- `ne`, `nu` and `nn` are the rows of the data in each set.
- `tests` shows, for every row, the Shapiro-Wilk and Levene p-values and the set it was sorted into.

Let's look at the ANOVA results.

```{r anova results}
head(res$anova_results)
```

The table starts with the ANOVA p-values for each main effect and their interaction. Then, for each pair of groups, it has the pairwise (here Tukey) p-value, the adjusted p-value and the log2 fold change. It ends with the mean of each group and the name of the pairwise test.

Two kinds of p-value adjustment are involved:

- The pairwise p-values (Tukey, Dunnett T3, Dunn) are already adjusted for comparing several pairs of groups within one row.
- The `padj` columns adjust for testing many rows, using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. They are calculated separately within each set. They can be turned off with `padj = FALSE`.

The Welch and Kruskal-Wallis results have the same layout, except that they start with a single `pvalue` and `padj`, because those tests compare all the combined groups at once.

```{r welch results}
head(res$welch_results)
```

To see how each row was sorted:

```{r tests}
head(res$tests)
table(res$tests$set)
```

All the pairwise results can be combined into one table, because they have the same columns in all three sets:

```{r combine results}
pairwise <- lapply(res[c("anova_results", "welch_results", "kw_results")], function(tab) {
    tab[, grep("_vs_|_mean$|^test$", colnames(tab))]
})
all_results <- do.call(rbind, unname(pairwise))
head(all_results)
```

## Part 2: Two-group, one-factor design

First, load the data. For this example we'll look at gene expression data from an RNA-seq experiment, normalized by DESeq2. There are two groups in this data set: samples 1-4 and samples 5-8. For the purposes of this example, we'll call them "treated" and "untreated".

```{r read in}
x <- read.csv("two_group_normalized_counts.csv")
x <- cf(x)
head(x)
```

Now we make the `sample_info` to map our samples to their group.

```{r sample_info}
sample_info <- data.frame(sample = colnames(x),
                          group = c(rep("treated", 4), rep("untreated", 4)))
sample_info
```

For two groups we use `twogroup_main()`, with the name of the column that holds the groups.

```{r twogroup_main}
res <- twogroup_main(x, sample_info, factors = "group")
names(res)
```

The results are in `ttest_results`, `welch_results` and `wilcox_results`. Each has the p-value, the adjusted p-value, the log2 fold change, the two group means and the name of the test:

```{r twogroup results}
head(res$ttest_results)
```

Because all three tables have the same columns, they can be combined directly:

```{r twogroup combine}
all_results <- rbind(res$ttest_results, res$welch_results, res$wilcox_results)
head(all_results)
```

## Part 3: Multi-group, one-factor design

The data used here is species-level data from a metagenomic analysis. There are 24 samples in three groups, with 8 samples per group. We'll call the groups group1, group2 and group3. This analysis moves a bit faster, as the steps are the same as before.

```{r species data}
x <- read.csv("species_abundance.csv")
x <- cf(x)
head(x)
sample_info <- data.frame(sample = colnames(x),
                          group = c(rep("group1", 8), rep("group2", 8), rep("group3", 8)))
```

```{r species analysis}
set.seed(1)
res <- multigroup_main(x, sample_info, factors = "group")
```

With a single factor, statomatic uses a one-way ANOVA for the ne rows, and the ANOVA results start with a single `pvalue` and `padj`, like the Welch and Kruskal-Wallis results.

```{r species results}
head(res$anova_results)
```
